utterance: G'day Mark, I'm Dr. Rao. Thanks for coming in. I can see you're not looking too good — let's sort out what's going on. Can you walk me through it from the start? How many days have you had this cough and fever, and have you measured your temperature at home — how high has it gone?
reply: It has been three days now. It was a dry, hacking cough to start with, but since yesterday I am bringing stuff up that is a rusty, brownish colour, though it was clear at first. I have been burning up on and off, and while I did not have a thermometer, I was roasting.

awards.label: Chest pain with breathing or coughing

utterance: Thanks, that's helpful. A rust-coloured cough can point to an infection deeper in the chest, so let me ask about a few red flags. Do you have any pain in your chest, especially when you take a deep breath or cough? Have you felt short of breath at all — like at rest, or with normal activity like walking to the office? And have you had any shivers or rigors — those whole-body shaking chills?
reply: There is a sharp pain low down on the right side, round towards my back that catches me when I take a deep breath or cough, and it started yesterday. I only get puffed going up the stairs and on the way in from the car park, but sitting here I am alright, and the first night I was shaking under the doona with my teeth chattering even though I was boiling. I do not know the word rigors, so what does that mean?

utterance:
No worries — a "rigor" is just one of those shivering episodes you described, and they're a clue to a bacterial infection in the chest. The pain you're describing on the right side, catching with breathing, fits with the lining of the lung being irritated. 

A few more history points: did this start with any sore throat, runny nose or general aches first — or did the fever and cough just hit you? How are you managing at home — can you drink normally, and are you going to the toilet a normal amount? Do you smoke, or drink a fair bit of alcohol? And do you have any other health problems, take any regular medications, or have any drug allergies?
reply: I was fine until three days ago, and my wife and our two teenagers are at home with me. I have never smoked, and I have a couple of beers on the weekend, though none this week. I am allergic to penicillin because I came up in hives and my lips swelled when I was a kid.

awards.label: A flu-like illness in the weeks before

utterance: Thanks, that confirms what the exam suggested. Paracetamol for fever and chest pain

utterance:
Here's what's going on, Mark. The exam and the X-ray both show an area of pneumonia in the lower part of your right lung — the fluid and air bronchograms on the film, plus the dullness and crackles I found, all point to that. It's most likely a common bacterial pneumonia, and it fits the whole picture: fever with rigors, the rust-coloured cough, and the one-sided pain with breathing. I've also checked and ruled out a fluid build-up or a blood clot in the lung, and your heart and the rest of the X-ray look normal.

Your symptoms aren't severe — your blood pressure and oxygen are okay and you're quite well otherwise — so you can be safely treated at home. Because of that penicillin allergy, I've started you on doxycycline instead: take two 100 mg tablets together today, then one tablet each morning for the next four days, so five days in total. Take it with a full glass of water, stay upright for half an hour after, and take it one hour before or two hours after milk or antacids. It makes your skin more sensitive to the sun, so wear a hat and sleeves in the sun while on it. Finish the whole course even if you feel better, and skip the beer while you're on it.

For the fever and aches, take 1 g of paracetamol — that's two 500 mg tablets — every 6–8 hours as needed, no more than four times a day. Keep drinking fluids and rest; there's no need to keep staying in bed, but ease back into teaching over a few days.

A few things to watch for. It's normal to still feel off and have a lingering cough, and the fever should start settling within 48 to 72 hours of starting the antibiotic. Call us for a same-day review if you're not noticeably better by the day after tomorrow. Go to the emergency department sooner if: you're breathing faster or more distressed, the chest pain worsens, you see frank blood in the sputum, you feel confused or very drowsy, your lips or fingertips look blue, or you can't keep fluids down. And if the cough still hasn't settled after about six weeks, come back for a repeat X-ray to make sure it's fully resolved.
reply: Pneumonia sounds pretty serious, but at least I can go home and get this sorted out before exams start.
